newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algerians to elect first multi-party parliament.
newsitem.headline: Algerians to elect first multi-party parliament.

text.p: Millions of Algerians vote on Thursday in the first parliamentary election since the North African country was plunged into violence five years ago.
Algerian armed forces on Wednesday stepped up security across the country to try to avert any attempts by Islamist guerrillas to sabotage the polling.
Nearly 17 million people are eligible to choose from more than 7,700 candidates representing 39 political parties for the 380-seat National Assembly (lower house).
More than 37,500 polling stations will open from 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) to 7 p.m. (1800 GMT) although local authorities may extend polling hours in some centres to help voters.
Once elected, the new parliament will be the first to group several political parties in the oil and gas producing country.

President Liamine Zeroual's government says the poll is key to ending the civil strife which erupted after the army-backed authorities cancelled in January 1992 general elections the radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) was poised to win.
An estimated 60,000 people have been killed since.

Heavily armed troops and police, backed by armoured troop carriers, increased the number of roadblocks on the entrances of Algiers and in some streets near the city centre where Moslem rebels have been active in the past, witnesses said.
Armed plaincloth police deployed at polling stations but witnesses said the deployment was of a lower profile than during the presidential election of November 1995.

The stepped-up security follows a bombing campaign in the capital by suspected Moslem rebels in which 22 people were killed and 120 wounded. The last of three explosions targeting buses was on Monday.
No major rebel attacks have been reported since.
State-run radio repeated on Wednesday an interior ministry statement urging civilians to report all suspicious vehicles or packages at bus stops and crowded streets.
The authorities earlier this week ordered all weekly markets and some schools to close until after the election. An old ban on parking cars in crowded streets was also reinforced.

The frontrunners at the elections are the National Democratic Rally (RNP), which groups Zeroual supporters, and the Islam-oriented Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS) of moderate Islamist leader Mahfoud Nahnah.
Other leading parties include the Socialist Forces Front (FFS) of secularist opposition leader Hocine Ait Ahmed and the Rally for Culture and Democracy of anti-Islamist Said Saadi.
A new proprotional representation law virtually guarantees that at least four or five parties will be in parliament with little chance of a single party holding an absolute majority.
An independent election commission, headed by former nationalist leader Salah Boubnider and with representatives of 21 parties, will supervise the poll.
More than 250 officials from the Organisation of African Unity and the Arab League as well as four from the United Nations, will also monitoring the voting.
